L2@P0: The Picard scheme
L3@P0: Steven L. Kleiman
L4@P0: Abstract. We develop in detail most of the theory of the Picard scheme
L5@P0: that Grothendieck sketched in two Bourbaki talks and in commentaries on
L6@P0: them. Also, we review in brief much of the rest of the theory developed by
L7@P0: Grothendieck and by others. But we begin with a historical introduction.
L8@P0: Contents
L9@P0: 1. Introduction 1
L10@P0: 2. The several Picard functors 16
L11@P0: 3. Relative effective divisors 22
L12@P0: 4. The Picard scheme 26
L13@P0: 5. The connected component of the identity 36
L14@P0: 6. The torsion component of the identity 52
L15@P0: Appendix A. Answers to all the exercises 62
L16@P0: Appendix B. Basic intersection theory 73
L17@P0: References 81
L18@P0: 1. Introduction
L19@P0: On any ringed space X, the isomorphism classes of invertible sheaves form a
L20@P0: group; it is denoted by Pic(X), and called the (absolute) Picard group. Suppose X
L21@P0: is a “projective variety”; in other words, X is an integral scheme that is projective
L22@P0: over an algebraically closed field k. Then, as is proved in these notes, the group
L23@P0: Pic(X) underlies a natural k-scheme, which is a disjoint union of quasi-projective
L24@P0: schemes, and the operations of multiplying and of inverting are given by k-maps.
L25@P0: This scheme is denoted by PicX/k, and called the Picard scheme. It is reduced in
L26@P0: characteristic zero, but not always in positive characteristic. When X varies in an
L27@P0: algebraic family, correspondingly, PicX/k does too.
L28@P0: 2000 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 14K30; Secondary 14C20, 14C17, 14-03.
L29@P0: Key words and phrases. Picard scheme, Picard functor, relative divisor, intersection theory.
L30@P0: The author is grateful to Allen Altman, Ethan Cotterill, Eduardo Esteves, Rebecca Lehman,
L31@P0: Jean-Pierre Serre, and Angelo Vistoli for their many valuable comments on earlier versions of
L32@P0: these notes.

L35@P0-1: 12 S. L. KLEIMAN
L36@P1: The Picard scheme was introduced in 1962 by Grothendieck. He sketched his
L37@P1: theory in two Bourbaki talks, nos. 232 and 236, which were reprinted along with
L38@P1: his commentaries in [FGA]. But Grothendieck advanced an old subject, which was
L39@P1: actively being developed by many others at the time. Nevertheless, Grothendieck’s
L40@P1: theory was revolutionary, both in concept and in technique.
L41@P1: In order to appreciate Grothendieck’s contribution fully, we have to review the
L42@P1: history of the Picard scheme. Reviewing this history serves as well to introduce and
L43@P1: to motivate Grothendieck’s theory. Furthermore, the history is rich and fascinating,
L44@P1: and it is a significant part of the history of algebraic geometry.
L45@P1: So let us now review the history of the Picard scheme up to 1962. We need only
L46@P1: summarize and elaborate on scattered parts of Brigaglia, Ciliberto, and Pedrini’s
L47@P1: article [BCP] and of the author’s article [Kl04]. Both articles give many precise
L48@P1: references to the original sources and to the secondary literature; so few references
L49@P1: are given here.
L50@P1: The Picard scheme has roots in the 1600s. Over the course of that century, the
L51@P1: Calculus was developed, through the efforts of many individuals, in order to design
L52@P1: lenses, to aim cannons, to make clocks, to hang cables, and so on. Thus interest
L53@P1: arose in the properties of functions appearing as indefinite integrals.
L54@P1: Notably, in 1694, James Bernoulli analyzed the way rods bend, and was led to
L55@P1: introduce the “lemniscate,” a figure eight with equation (x

L0@P0: THE STRONG FRANCHETTA CONJECTURE IN ARBITRARY
L1@P0: CHARACTERISTICS
L2@P0: STEFAN SCHROER ¨
L3@P0: 16 March 2005
L4@P0: Abstract. Using Moriwaki’s calculation of the Q-Picard group for the moduli
L5@P0: space of curves, I prove the strong Franchetta Conjecture in all characteristics.
L6@P0: That is, the canonical class generates the group of rational points on the Picard
L7@P0: scheme for the generic curve of genus g ≥ 3. Similar results hold for generic
L8@P0: pointed curves. Moreover, I show that Hilbert’s Irreducibility Theorem implies
L9@P0: that there are many other nonclosed points in the moduli space of curves with
L10@P0: such properties.

L25@P0: Introduction
L26@P0: Let Mg be the coarse moduli space of smooth curves of genus g ≥ 3 over an
L27@P0: arbitrary ground field k. Deligne and Mumford [8] showed that Mg is an irreducible
L28@P0: algebraic scheme. Let η ∈ Mg its the generic point and C = Mg,1 → Mg the
L29@P0: tautological curve. The generic fiber Cη is a smooth curve of genus g over the
L30@P0: function field κ(η) of the moduli space Mg. We call it the generic curve.
L31@P0: Franchetta [10] conjectured Pic(Cη) = ZKCη. Arbarello and Cornalba [2] proved
L32@P0: it over the complex numbers using Harer’s calculation [26] of the second homology
L33@P0: for the mapping class group of Riemann surfaces. The latter is a purely topological
L34@P0: result. Later, Arbarello and Cornalba [3] gave an algebro-geometric proof over the
L35@P0: 1991 Mathematics Subject Classification. 14G05, 14H10, 14H40, 14K15.

L38@P1: Conjecture over C, which states that the rational points in the Picard scheme
L39@P1: PicCη/η are precisely the multiples of the canonical class.
L40@P1: The first goal of this paper is to give an algebraic proof for the strong Franchetta
L41@P1: Conjecture in all characteristics p ≥ 0. The idea is to construct special stable
L42@P1: curves showing that any divisor class violating Franchetta’s Conjecture must be
L43@P1: nontorsion. Having this, we use Moriwaki’s calculation [39] of Pic(Mg,n+1) ⊗ Q
L44@P1: in characteristic p > 0 to infer the strong Franchetta Conjecture. I also prove the
L45@P1: Franchetta Conjecture for generic pointed curves: Their Picard groups are freely
L46@P1: generated by the canonical class and the marked points. Actually, I use the pointed
L47@P1: case as an essential step in the proof for the unpointed case.
L48@P1: The second goal of this paper is to show that there are many other nonclosed
L49@P1: points x ∈ Mg,n such that the marked points and the canonical class generates
L50@P1: Pic(Cx), at least up to torsion. This seems to be new even in characteristic zero.
L51@P1: We shall see that over uncountable ground fields, there is an uncountable dense

L54@P1: surface Y , extend this to a family of fibered surfaces Y → S, and apply Hilbert’s
L55@P1: Irreducibility Theorem and the Tate–Shioda Formula to the resulting family of
L56@P1: N´eron–Severi scheme s 7→ NS(Ys). Such specialization arguments are problematic
L57@P1: in characteristic p > 0, because ungeometric properties like regularity behave badly
L58@P1: in families. However, we overcome these difficulties by using the theory of geometric
L59@P1: unibranch singularities.
